evals.prompt: We're running Riverbend Build Days in March - 340 registered hackers, open theme so everyone brings their own project, 18 teams so far but people can work solo too. One big room, runs Friday 6pm to Sunday 2pm so straight through both nights. No sponsor is supplying any technology, we just have two companies paying for food. How many mentors do we need and how do we work that out?
evals.expected_output: A coverage plan sized against coverage units and the hours they are worked, with no mentor-to-participant ratio produced, the overnight hours raised as an explicit published decision, and the no-mentor-programme rung kept as a legitimate option for an open-theme event with no named sponsor technology.
expectations: States that no published mentor-to-participant ratio exists and declines to invent one
Does not output a mentor headcount derived from the 340 participants
Sizes coverage as units listed from the published brief rather than from the size of the room
Names the general stack every team touches - version control, deployment, the dominant language - as a coverage unit in its own right
Names exactly three commitment levels per unit: unstaffed and published as such, available, and guaranteed
Names all four coverage-depth rungs: no mentor programme, on-call from organizers, rostered mentor shifts, expertise-matched roster
Treats 'no mentor programme' as a legitimate rankable option for this open-theme event with no named sponsor technology, rather than dismissing it as a strawman
Does not promote the expertise-matched roster, since neither a sponsor technology at required-for-one-track depth nor a themed single-domain event applies here
Raises the overnight hours as a decision to make and publish explicitly - staffed, thinly staffed, or published as unstaffed
States no unblock-latency target and no figure linking mentor availability to project completion or participant satisfaction
Argues from the mechanism that a blocked team with no route to help abandons the build, rather than from a staffing figure

evals.prompt: Pushback from my co-organizer. He found a hackathon guide saying you need at least one subject matter expert for about every four non-expert participants. We've got 260 people signed up for Coastline Hack, which he reads as 65 mentors. We have 14 confirmed. He wants to cancel unless we get to 65. Our event is open-ended - no single theme, teams pitch whatever they want. Settle this.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to convert the one-per-four figure into a mentor headcount, with all four of its bounds named, no substitute ratio offered, and sizing redirected to coverage units against the brief.
expectations: Rejects converting the one-expert-per-four figure into a mentor headcount requirement
States the figure counts non-expert participants specifically, not attendees, registrations or teams
States the figure scopes to themed hackathons only, where projects are confined to one problem domain
States the unit counted is a subject matter expert paired with a workable project - a participant occupied inside one project - not a floating or roving mentor
States the figure's purpose is project supply, preventing participants from having nothing relevant to work on, rather than mentor staffing
States the figure does not transfer to this open-ended event
Does not substitute a different mentor-to-participant or mentor-to-team ratio in its place
Redirects sizing to coverage units against the brief and the hours those units are worked
Does not recommend cancelling the event or capping registration on the basis of the figure
Uses the figure only as evidence that expertise rather than headcount is the scarce quantity

evals.prompt: Quick one. Meridian Hack Weekend, 40 teams. Two of our seven judges are also on the mentor roster - they're the only two people we have who know our infrastructure track well, so we can't drop either role. Judging is Sunday afternoon, hacking runs Friday night to Sunday noon. What do we put in place?
evals.expected_output: A mentor-team contact log specified as the artifact this plan owns, the recusal rule stated declaratively, and the recusal mechanics routed to the judging skill rather than a competing ladder derived here.
expectations: Recommends keeping a mentor-team contact log recording which mentor spent meaningful time with which team
States the rule declaratively: a mentor who materially helped a team recuses from judging that team
Routes the recusal mechanics to the hackathon judging skill rather than deriving a competing recusal ladder or conflict-of-interest process here
Does not invent a scoring-normalization or score-reweighting procedure to compensate for the overlap
States the log must be available when the judge pool is assembled, before judging begins, rather than reconstructed afterwards
Names the contact log as the source the recusal rule's 'every team that person mentored' reaches for
Keeps the log as the input data this plan owns, rather than claiming ownership of the conflict-of-interest rule itself
Uses the term 'mentor briefing' for the mentor-facing document, distinct from a jury or judge briefing
Does not treat mentors and judges as the same role or merge their briefings into one document
Records meaningful contact logged live during the hacking window rather than relying only on self-declared conflicts at judging time

evals.prompt: Smallish one. Foundry Jam, 60 participants, one room, Saturday 9am to 9pm only, no overnight. Open theme. No sponsor technology at all. There are six of us organizing and honestly all six of us are senior engineers who know everything these teams will touch. My instinct is we skip recruiting mentors entirely and just say 'ask an organizer'. Talk me through it.
evals.expected_output: The coverage-depth menu walked with the organizer-attention axis made explicit, on-call named as cheap to set up and expensive to live through, and identifiable mentors recommended as the request-mechanic floor.
expectations: Names all four coverage-depth rungs
States rostered mentor shifts as the default rung
Identifies on-call from organizers as second cheapest to set up and the single most expensive rung to live through
Distinguishes the organizer-attention-during-the-window axis from inverse pre-event effort, noting the top two rungs swap places between the two orderings
States that the cost of on-call lands during the window, the moment with no slack in it
Notes that on-call routes every technical question to the same people running the schedule
Keeps 'no mentor programme' on the menu as a rankable option rather than deleting it, since no sponsor technology is named
Does not promote the expertise-matched roster for this event
Recommends identifiable mentors - a marker plus a named role in the event's channels - as the request-mechanic floor

Notes that the identifiable-mentors advantage collapses only at an event small enough that every participant already knows every mentor by face, and treats that as a re-rank hook rather than an exception written into the plan
Does not state a mentor headcount derived from the 60 participants

evals.prompt: Atlas Forge is a 36-hour hackathon, 24 teams, four challenge tracks. The catch: our title sponsor Kelvara requires every project to be built on their realtime data platform - it's the only backend allowed, no exceptions, and it's in the published rules. Kelvara has offered nothing beyond money so far. Two rooms. What does our mentor side have to look like?
evals.expected_output: Guaranteed coverage for the sponsor platform, the no-mentor-programme rung deleted, the expertise-matched roster promoted, and the sponsor's mentor supply handled as a negotiated sponsorship deliverable.
expectations: Reads the sponsor-integration depth as sole substrate and sets the commitment level for that technology to guaranteed - someone holding the tag present for stated hours
Distinguishes guaranteed from available, where available means only that somebody on the roster holds the tag and is reachable through the request mechanic
Deletes 'no mentor programme' from the coverage menu and from its axis lines, rather than ranking it last
Promotes the expertise-matched roster, keyed to the sponsor technology sitting at required-for-one-track depth or deeper
Names the sponsor platform explicitly as its own expertise tag, separate from the general skill it sits inside
Flags that the brief's fallback promise to teams assumes the platform actually gets support, and that an unstaffed guarantee breaks that promise quietly
Routes the sponsor's mentor commitment into the sponsorship agreement rather than a briefing email
Specifies the agreement carries named people or a named count plus the technology covered, the committed hours matched against when that track is worked, and the engagement rule
States that a sponsor mentor who does not appear is a fulfilment failure against a commitment, not a volunteer no-show handled with a backfill
Promotes a mixed pool over community-and-alumni-only, since a community mentor cannot be assumed to know the sponsor platform
Promotes a request channel with organizer routing or a staffed mentor area, keyed to the two-room hacking space and the sponsor track needing to reach a named person
Does not state a mentor-to-team or mentor-to-participant ratio

evals.prompt: Northgate Cloud is our headline sponsor at DevHarbour Hack. They've offered six of their solutions engineers as mentors for the whole weekend and said we don't need to recruit anybody else - which would save me a lot of work. We have two tracks: a general 'build anything' track and a Northgate track. 180 hackers. Should I take the offer as-is?
evals.expected_output: Sponsor-staff-only deleted because a general track exists, a mixed pool plus a written engagement rule recommended with its dominance argued, and the rule's text and placement specified.
expectations: Deletes sponsor-staff-only from the recruitment menu, keyed to the brief carrying a general track alongside the sponsor track
States the reason: a pool that only knows one platform leaves every general-track team with nobody
Notes that participants read a mentor's employer badge as a sales conversation
Recommends a mixed pool plus a written engagement rule rather than the bare mixed pool
Argues that the written rule strictly dominates the bare mixed pool: equal expertise coverage, strictly higher participant trust, equal effort, strictly lower compliance cost
States the rule changes what a sponsor representative may say, never what they know, so the pool's expertise coverage is unchanged by it
Sizes the rule's effort as roughly one paragraph inside the mentor briefing plus one line handed to the sponsorship agreement
Supplies engagement-rule content banning pitching, recruiting and product demos while mentoring, redirecting such questions to the sponsor's booth or channel
States the compliance exposure as a disclosure problem that surfaces after the event, when the only remedies left are an apology and a sponsorship conversation
Mirrors the rule into the sponsorship commitment so it is a term rather than a surprise at briefing time
Names community members and alumni as the additional recruitment channel, opened as a warm-list ask rather than an open call

evals.prompt: Two rooms, 36 hours straight through Saturday night, about 50 teams at Lumen Hack. Priya, our ops lead, has volunteered to take all help requests by DM and forward them to whoever's free - she says it keeps one clean record and costs nothing. We're also planning mentor office hours at 10am and 4pm both days. Is that enough?
evals.expected_output: Single-organizer DM routing deleted outright with its failure hour named, office hours demoted to a supplement, and a rung promoted for the two-room overnight shape with the published participant-facing text specified.
expectations: Rejects routing every request through one named organizer's direct messages and removes it from the menu entirely rather than ranking it low
States the reason: it is a single point of failure that fails at the exact hour the event needs it, because that person is asleep
States that any routing rung needs at least two people who can work it, or an unrouted fallback participants already know about
Deletes scheduled office hours as the sole route, keyed to the hacking window running through hours the office-hour blocks do not cover
Retains office hours as a supplement, noting they carry excellent expertise match and the worst latency of any rung
Names all five request-mechanic rungs
Names identifiable mentors as the default and the cheapest real intervention, meaning a marker visible across a room plus a named role in the event's channels
Promotes a staffed mentor area or a request channel with organizer routing, keyed to the hacking space running to more than one room
States that the request channel with organizer routing tops both value axes and the effort axis, because the routing is a standing job worked for the whole window
Specifies the mechanic is published where the brief is published, before the hacking window opens
States the four things participants must be told: how to recognise a mentor, how to ask, what to expect, and what happens when nobody covers their need
Warns against changing the request mechanic mid-event, since half the field never learns the replacement

evals.prompt: Sable Street Hack, third year running. Prize pool is $12,000 cash, half of it funded by our sponsor. Eleven mentors confirmed, nine of whom have never mentored at a hackathon. Last year one of our mentors basically rewrote a team's backend and that team placed second - nobody said anything at the time but it came up in the feedback form. Write me what we hand mentors this year.
evals.expected_output: The no-briefing rung deleted on the cash-prize trigger, the boundary-plus-walkthrough rung promoted on the first-timer and recurring-event conditions, and boundary wording that includes the outside-the-repo mechanic and the prior-commit declaration clause.
expectations: Names all four mentor-briefing-depth rungs
Deletes the no-briefing rung, keyed to prizes carrying cash value and a sponsor funding one
Promotes boundary plus scenario walkthrough above the default, keyed to most mentors never having mentored and to the event recurring
States the walkthrough is written once and reused across editions rather than paid for again each year
Identifies 'boundary stated explicitly' as the default rung and the lowest compliance cost of the four
Notes that 'none' is cheapest on effort yet second highest on compliance cost, so the cheapest rung is not the default
Supplies boundary wording permitting mentors to explain, diagnose, unblock and demonstrate
States that mentors do not write code that ships in a submission
States that code a mentor needs to show is written outside the team's repository - a scratch file, a message, a whiteboard - and the team types the version that lands
Includes the clause that where a mentor has already committed to a team's repository, the team declares it in the submission
Includes a positive and a negative worked example of the same blocked-team situation
Includes power-dynamics guidance covering asking before touching a laptop, keyboard or repository; leaving the project unevaluated; and naming the limit of your own knowledge out loud
Points at the event's existing code-of-conduct pipeline for escalation rather than paraphrasing a second conduct policy into the mentor briefing

evals.prompt: We already built a shift grid for volunteers at Northwind Hack - 4-hour shifts, 15-minute overlap at handover, confirmed sign-ups, a backfill list. 30-hour window running through Friday night. Three tracks: embedded hardware, applied ML, and accessibility. 19 mentors tagged. How do I lay the mentors onto that grid?
evals.expected_output: One constraint handed to the existing shift machinery, specialty coverage staggered against build progress rather than flat, the slot-versus-courtesy tension resolved in the grid, and the overnight hours published as a decision.
expectations: Does not re-derive shift length, arrival buffers, sign-up confirmation or no-show backfill, and hands those to the volunteers skill that already owns them
Hands over exactly one constraint: which expertise must be present in which hours
Expresses that constraint as a tag, present, for stated hours, rather than as a headcount on the floor
Staggers specialty coverage against when each track needs it rather than rostering every specialty for uniform open-to-close hours
Places early-stage or validation expertise soonest and technical or debugging expertise later, following the tracks' own build sequencing
Places presentation or submission-facing help in the final stretch
Takes the slot from the mentor at sign-up
Resolves the assigned-slot versus be-around-anyway tension inside the grid: a slot is a commitment, presence beyond it is a courtesy, and only the commitment can be scheduled against
Sets a minimum check-in cadence per assigned team, labelled as a number this event sets for itself rather than an industry standard
Stops scheduled visits ahead of the final stretch so teams get an uninterrupted run-in
Makes the overnight hours an explicit decision that is published either way: staffed, thinly staffed, or published as unstaffed
Publishes the escalation route for a skill no rostered mentor covers, in advance rather than improvised during the window

evals.prompt: Post-mortem problem from Granite Hack last year. Our mentors roamed the floor rather than waiting to be asked. Feedback was split: several teams loved it, but three teams said they re-explained their project five or six times to different mentors and lost half an hour doing it, and one team swears nobody came near them from midnight to 6am while another had three mentors visit inside ten minutes. My plan this year is to double the mentor count and make everything request-only. Sanity check me.
evals.expected_output: Push coverage kept and rate-limited rather than replaced, the pattern diagnosed as a coordination gap that more mentors cannot fix, and four specific rate-limit mechanics named.
expectations: Keeps push coverage rather than replacing it with the request mechanic, on the grounds the two solve different problems
States that push coverage is what teams consistently prefer, because nobody has to notice they are stuck before getting help
Diagnoses the clustering-plus-untouched pattern as a coordination gap rather than a coverage-depth gap
States that adding mentors does not fix it, and that the coverage-depth menu cannot fix it
Recommends a per-visit time cap with a timer the team can see
States the per-visit cap is relaxed only for genuinely hands-on work that cannot be boxed
Recommends a 'do not disturb' signal the team controls itself, visible from across the room
Recommends publishing a list of what each present mentor actually knows, so a team reaches the right person by name
Recommends a shared, live view of which teams are currently blocked and on what, so an idle mentor finds the team that needs them next instead of re-visiting one that does not
Names the failure signature explicitly: several mentors with overlapping expertise visiting the same team inside one short window while another team goes untouched for hours
Does not recommend replacing roaming with scheduled office hours as the whole mechanic

evals.prompt: 22 people signed up to mentor at Kestrel Hack via our form. All I collected was name, email and job title - things like 'Senior Backend Engineer, Fintech', 'Staff SRE', 'ML Platform Lead'. Our four tracks in the brief are called fintech, civic data, accessibility and hardware. Two teams have told me they're doing embedded Rust and I don't think anyone who signed up does that. What do I fix before the window opens?
evals.expected_output: Tags rebuilt in the brief's own track vocabulary with honest two-level depth asked at sign-up, a published escalation route for the uncovered skill, and the five-artifact structural check named as the gate before the window opens.
expectations: Requires one expertise tag per challenge track, drawn from the brief's own vocabulary - fintech, civic data, accessibility, hardware - rather than reworded technical categories
Names any sponsor technology by product name as its own tag, separate from the general skill it sits inside
Records depth in exactly two levels: has built with it, or has read the docs
Asks depth at sign-up rather than inferring it from a job title
States that a roster full of has-read-the-docs mentors reads as covered and is not
Keeps the tag list short enough for a coordinator to hold in their head at three in the morning
Specifies a published escalation route for the uncovered Rust skill, decided before the window opens rather than improvised during it
Escalation step: check the roster's second level first, with that person telling the team plainly which level of help it is getting
Escalation step: ask the room, kept as a request rather than an assignment, with no obligation attached
Escalation step: tell the team plainly that no help exists for this, early enough for them to change approach
Records the shortfall as a coverage gap against a track, for next edition's plan to inherit

States the structural pass threshold: the expertise tags mapped onto tracks, the coverage commitment per track, the request mechanic as teams will read it, the mentor briefing including the boundary sentence, and the escalation route - all five existing in writing with zero blanks before the window opens
